problem: Existing LLM-based VLN agents (NavGPT, MapGPT, DiscussNav) cannot selectively recall and apply relevant prior navigation experience, so they pick arbitrarily among visually similar candidate viewpoints and do poorly on long-horizon, unfamiliar scenes.
motivation: Experienced human navigators recall familiar routes and salient landmarks and remember their first mistakes. LLMs have broad general knowledge but struggle to ground it in specific spatial contexts, and their reasoning over navigation information lacks structure. A retrievable, continually updated experience memory could fix this.
key_idea: Build a viewpoint-level multimodal experience memory (panorama + landmark text, CLIP/FAISS indexed), retrieve relevant past cases at each step and turn them into a high-priority navigation rule in the prompt, and update the memory after each episode through reflection (whole successful paths, only the first error for failures).
insight: Retrieved experience helps only when it is injected as an explicit high-priority rule: treated as ordinary context (w/o NR), SR drops from 56 to 48.2 and SPL by over 10 points, to roughly MapGPT level, so the LLM largely ignores it. Replacing reflected experiences with fixed scene descriptions (w/ SD) is worst (SR 40, NE 10.20) because the LLM tries to align the text to the observation and circles in place. What is stored (trajectories and first-error notes) matters more than richer descriptions.
method: Multimodal Experience Memory (MEM): one memory unit per Matterport3D viewpoint, storing the panoramic SkyBox image, viewpoint ID, and salient landmark texts detected by a fine-tuned Detic; CLIP image and text embeddings form a hybrid embedding indexed with FAISS.

Instruction-aware attention fusion: CLIP embeddings of the K candidate view images are fused into one observation embedding v_obs, with softmax weights alpha_k = softmax(u^T W v_k) from the instruction embedding u, instead of mean pooling.

Retrieval and rule generation: cosine similarity between v_obs and the FAISS embeddings gives the best memory unit E*, which is converted into an explicit navigation rule R (failure cases also include the panorama of the first wrong step).

RAG prompt pipeline (RAGP): the prompt manager PM = {I, O, H, M; R} combines instruction, candidate images, history of (id, rationale), and an incrementally built MapGPT-style semantic topological map. R is a privileged constraint. GPT-4o outputs analysis, multi-step plan, and next viewpoint.

Reflection and memory update: after each episode, success or failure is judged. Successful cases store the instruction and full trajectory in every viewpoint unit on the path. Failures store only the first wrong decision (viewpoint, rationale, type: mid-route deviation, false goal recognition, or post-goal continuation).

Experience filter: a new successful route is discarded if a similar, more efficient one exists, otherwise it replaces the worse one. A failure entry is ignored if its decision point and reason are already stored.
Real-robot adaptation: the scene is partitioned into landmark-based regions, each treated as a memory unit, with low-level primitives (forward 50 cm, turn 45°).

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) with CLIP encoders, fine-tuned Detic, FAISS retrieval; the attention projection W is described as learned
setting.training_data: none (training-free / zero-shot) apart from the Detic fine-tuning; the memory is filled online from the agent's own episodes
setting.observation: Matterport3D panoramic RGB and candidate-view RGB images; monocular RGB on the real robot
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints in simulation; low-level primitives (move forward 50 cm, turn left 45°) on the real robot
setting.simulator: Matterport3D simulator (R2R); real world with TurtleBot 4 Lite
setting.privileged: Success/failure judged against ground-truth goal location during reflection to update memory (evaluation-time feedback); otherwise none

numbers_note: Table I is labelled as the full val-unseen split, but the text does not say how the reflective memory was populated on the full split or whether the update order affects results. The ablation table values differ from Table I because they use a 216-episode subset.
results: On R2R val-unseen, CMMR-VLN gets SR 52 / SPL 51 / NE 5.10 / OSR 63, beating DiscussNav (SR 43, SPL 40), MapGPT (SR 43, SPL 34) and NavGPT (SR 34). On a TurtleBot 4 Lite with 20 instructions it reaches SR 30 against 10 (NavGPT) and 20 (MapGPT, DiscussNav).
limitations: Performance depends on the quality and coverage of stored experience, and the memory is built per viewpoint or region.

The real-robot evaluation is tiny (20 instructions, SR 30 vs 20), and the R2R evaluation relies on ground-truth success feedback to update memory, so the comparison with memory-less baselines may not be fully fair.
Uses only GPT-4o with no comparison against trained or fine-tuned VLN models, and gives no analysis of retrieval latency, API cost, or memory growth.
